ISSUE:


Description
Allow authenticated Stat'sTheGame users to request API consumer access rather than requiring an administrator to create every API consumer without a user-initiated request.

The current API-consumer lifecycle is administrator-driven. Administrators create consumer records and immediately receive a raw API key. Consumer ownership is also associated with the administrator account that created the consumer.

Introduce a user-requested access lifecycle with a clear separation between:

requesting API access;
administrator approval or rejection;
creation/ownership of the API consumer;
generation of credentials by the approved consumer owner; and
subsequent key and usage management.
A raw API key must not be generated as a side effect of administrator approval. After approval, the approved owner should explicitly generate their key while present so that the existing one-time-secret model can be preserved.

The consumer record must belong to the user/application receiving API access, not to the administrator who approved the request.

Motivation
External consumers currently have no in-product mechanism to request API access.

Requiring administrators to create every consumer manually:

provides no formal request or approval record;
makes onboarding dependent on an out-of-band conversation;
associates ownership with the issuing administrator rather than the consumer;
makes it difficult to provide consumer self-service usage/key management; and
encourages the administrator to receive a credential that should ultimately belong to the external consumer.
A request-and-approval workflow provides an auditable access lifecycle while retaining administrator control over who receives managed API capacity.

Acceptance Criteria
Consumer access requests
An authenticated eligible user can request API consumer access from the application.
A request records the requesting application user.
A request records a consumer/application name.
A request records a short intended-use description.
Request fields are validated server-side.
The request lifecycle has explicit pending, approved and rejected states.
Duplicate active/pending requests that violate the documented lifecycle are rejected consistently.
A rejected request does not grant any API capability.
The requester can see the current state of their own request.
A rejection can be followed by a new request according to the documented lifecycle.
Administrator review
Administrators can list pending API consumer access requests.
Administrators can inspect the safe information required to make an access decision.
Administrators can approve a pending request.
Administrators can reject a pending request.
Approval records the approving administrator and decision timestamp.
Rejection records the rejecting administrator and decision timestamp.
Any supported review reason is retained with the decision.
Administrator decisions are enforced by the backend rather than frontend state.
Consumer ownership
Approval creates or activates an API consumer owned by the requesting user, not the administrator who approved the request.
Consumer ownership is represented separately from approval/review metadata.
Administrators can administer consumer accounts independently of which administrator approved them.
Existing administrator-owner assumptions in the API-consumer repository are removed or migrated safely.
Ordinary users cannot inspect or manage another user's consumer.
Key issuance and management
Approval does not automatically generate or expose a raw API key to the administrator.
An approved consumer owner can explicitly generate their first API key.
The raw key is returned only as part of the successful generation response.
The raw key is displayed only once in the frontend.
Leaving or dismissing the one-time-key view removes the raw key from frontend state.
Raw keys are never stored in browser storage.
Raw keys are never persisted by the backend.
Only the existing non-reversible key representation and safe metadata are persisted.
An owner can rotate their own active consumer key.
Rotation invalidates the prior active credential according to the existing key policy.
An owner can revoke their own API key.
Administrators retain the ability to revoke consumer credentials when required.
Revoked credentials return the same generic unauthorized response as unknown credentials.
Consumer account experience
The signed-in account area exposes an API-access section.
A user without API access is shown the option to request it.
A pending request is clearly identified as awaiting administrator review.
A rejected request is represented clearly and permits the documented next action.
An approved user can see their consumer configuration without exposing a stored raw key.
An approved owner can generate/rotate/revoke credentials through an accessible workflow.
An approved owner can inspect their existing API usage information.
The interface explains the configured per-minute rate limit and daily quota.
Limits and administration
The administrator can set or confirm the approved consumer's per-minute rate limit and daily quota.
User-facing controls cannot increase their own approved limits.
Limit changes require administrator authorization.
The behaviour of consumers whose owning application account is disabled or deleted is explicitly defined and tested.
Active credentials cannot continue providing unintended access after the owning consumer has lost API access.
Security and privacy
API access requests cannot be used to grant application administrator or submission permissions.
A consumer API key authorizes only the documented API-consumer capabilities.
API consumer credentials are not accepted as bearer authentication for normal user/admin operations.
Supabase bearer authentication is not accepted as a substitute for a consumer API key on consumer-only operations.
Key values, hashes, authorization headers and other credentials are excluded from logs and telemetry.
Usage telemetry continues to contain only the existing safe consumer/key identifiers and normalized request information.
Testing and documentation
Database tests cover request persistence, ownership, approval, rejection and invalid lifecycle transitions.
API tests cover requester authorization and administrator authorization.
API tests cover first key generation, rotation and revocation.
API tests prove that one user cannot manage another user's consumer.
Frontend tests cover request, pending, rejected, approved and key-management states.
Keyboard and responsive behaviour are covered for the new user/admin workflows where applicable.
OpenAPI documents all new endpoints and schemas.
Consumer-key documentation explains the complete request → approval → credential-generation lifecycle.
API Explorer onboarding guidance points users to the new API-access request workflow.
Database documentation is updated for any new request/review fields or tables.
Existing unaffected tests continue to pass.
Dependency
The ownership and access behaviour must follow the decision recorded by the consumer API access-model issue.

docs/ai/usage.md and evidence/ai/registers/README.md as authoritative
where their rules apply, but do not reread them mechanically for every
issue.

If the requested implementation conflicts with an approved document or ADR,
stop and report the conflict.

## 4. Git workflow

Follow docs/git-methodology.md.

Never develop directly on `main`.

A development branch must follow:

<type>/<issue-number>-<short-description>

Use one issue per branch unless project methodology explicitly permits
otherwise.

Every normal development commit must reference:

Refs #<issue-number>

Do not push, merge, close an issue, or create/merge a Pull Request unless
Nadav explicitly requests it.

Never force-push main.

## 5. Architecture and implementation

Respect documented repository boundaries.

Do not bypass the handwritten backend HTTP API for application data.

Do not introduce alternative authentication, application-data APIs,
backends, frameworks or libraries where the project has already selected
an approach.

Before creating a new abstraction, dependency or pattern, check whether an
existing one fits.

Preserve behaviour and public interfaces outside the requested change.

Do not weaken tests to make an implementation pass.

## 6. Investigation efficiency

Use targeted searches.

After locating the affected area, inspect:

- the implementation;
- directly related tests;
- immediate dependencies or abstractions required to understand it.

Do not broadly inspect unrelated directories, documentation or Git history.

Do not repeatedly reread files or retry unchanged commands.

## 7. Testing

Behavioural changes require relevant tests using existing project
conventions.

During development:

- run the smallest relevant test or test file;
- use focused failures while debugging;
- run workspace-level checks where useful.

Do not repeatedly run repository-wide test/check/build suites while
developing.

When implementation is stable:

1. run focused tests proving the acceptance criteria;
2. run relevant workspace lint/typecheck/build checks;
3. run the relevant E2E specification where required;
4. run any broader project quality gate required for this change once.

If a broad check fails, isolate the failure with a focused command, fix it,
then rerun the required broad check after the implementation is stable.

Do not run unrelated suites merely because they exist.

Never claim a check passed unless it actually ran successfully.

If an applicable check cannot run, state exactly why.

## 8. Environment failures

Do not spend significant issue time repairing unrelated local environment
problems.

For an environment-only failure:

- diagnose enough to identify the blocker;
- do not repeatedly retry the same unchanged command;
- continue with verification that remains possible;
- report the limitation.

## 9. Documentation changes

Update documentation only when the issue changes behaviour, setup, API
contracts, database schema, security behaviour, deployment or another
documented interface.

Do not update documentation solely because implementation files changed.

## 10. AI attribution

Follow the course AI policy, docs/ai/usage.md and
evidence/ai/registers/README.md.

For material Codex work retained in the project, update only:

evidence/ai/registers/nadav-sundy.csv

Use only the actual tool/model used. Never invent verification, transcript,
PR or commit information.

Do not claim Nadav personally reviewed or verified AI output unless he
explicitly confirms it.

A commit containing Codex-generated or materially modified code must use:

Assisted-by: Codex[<exact active model>]

If multiple AI tools/models materially contributed to retained code, include
all required attribution.

If the exact model cannot be established when attribution is required, stop
and ask Nadav.

## 11. Completion

Before reporting completion:

1. compare the final implementation against every acceptance criterion;
2. inspect `git diff` for unrelated changes;
3. run the required final verification;
4. confirm every changed file is necessary;
5. handle required AI attribution/register updates.

Report concisely:

- acceptance criteria and evidence;
- changed files;
- checks actually run and results;
- documentation changes;
- limitations or deliberate follow-up work;
- proposed commit message(s);
- PR title and description.

When all locally performable work is finished, say:

"Implementation ready for review"

Do not describe the Gitea issue itself as complete until the project's formal
Definition of Done has been satisfied.

Do not perform review, PR creation, merge or issue closure unless Nadav asks.

Implemented issue #822 on `feat/822-api-consumer-access-requests`.

### Acceptance-criteria verification

- Authenticated users can submit validated API-access requests with application name and intended use.
- Pending, approved, and rejected lifecycle states are persisted and exposed to requesters.
- Pending/approved duplicates are rejected; rejected users can submit a new request.
- Administrators can inspect, approve, or reject pending requests with reviewer, timestamp, reason, rate limit, and quota metadata.
- Approval creates a consumer owned by the requester and does not generate a key.
- Owners explicitly generate their first key, rotate it, revoke it, and inspect usage.
- Raw keys are returned once, held only in component state, cleared when dismissed, and never persisted or stored in browser storage.
- Cross-user consumer management is rejected; administrators retain independent limit and revocation controls.
- Disabled/deleted owners can no longer authenticate with consumer credentials.
- Consumer keys remain isolated from normal user/admin bearer authentication.
- Account and administrator workflows cover responsive layout, keyboard interaction, and accessibility.
- OpenAPI, consumer-key lifecycle, API overview, migration, database schema, and API Explorer onboarding documentation were updated.

    )

)

    ON api_consumer_access_request (created_at, api_consumer_access_request_id)
    WHERE request_state = 'pending';

    'Audited user request and administrator decision; ownership remains on api_consumer.owner_app_user_id.';

    'Approved external API consumers owned by the application user operating the integration.';

    'Hashed consumer API keys. Raw material is returned once on explicit owner generation or rotation and is never persisted.';
;

content.text:
Improve the visual design and UX of the API access request page and the admin pending API access requests interface shown in the attached screenshots.
Before making changes, read and follow the repository's approved frontend/brand documentation, especially:
- docs/design/brand-guidelines.md
- any relevant frontend/component/accessibility guidelines under docs/
- existing shared components and styles already used elsewhere in the application
Do not redesign the overall product or invent a new visual language. This should bring these screens into alignment with the existing Stat’sTheGame design system.
Current problems
The current screens are functional but visually unfinished:
- Form controls are laid out almost entirely in one horizontal row.
- Labels run directly into inputs, making fields difficult to scan.
- Native-looking inputs/textareas/buttons clash with the rest of the application.
- There is very little hierarchy between page headings, explanatory text, request details, fields and actions.
- The admin request interface is extremely wide and sparse.
- Approve and reject controls sit beside one another without enough visual separation or hierarchy.
- The admin view does not visually group each pending request as a coherent review unit.
- Spacing is inconsistent and does not follow the brand spacing scale.
- The layout will not translate cleanly to smaller screens.
- Destructive and primary actions should be easier to distinguish without relying solely on colour.
Brand requirements
Follow the approved Stat’sTheGame brand system.
Use the existing semantic CSS tokens rather than introducing arbitrary colours or hard-coded theme values.
For Day Match, the relevant existing visual language includes:
- warm canvas background;
- Scorecard Paper surfaces;
- Match Ink text rather than pure black;
- Crease Green for the dominant primary action;
- Rejected Red only for genuinely destructive/rejection actions;
- restrained 1px structural borders;
- broad, subtle shadows where elevation is useful.
The same components must also work correctly in Night Match using the corresponding semantic tokens. Do not create light-theme-only styles.
Typography must follow the design system:
- Barlow Condensed for page/section headings;
- IBM Plex Sans for interface text, labels and form content;
- IBM Plex Mono only for genuinely technical values such as IDs where monospacing communicates meaning.
Follow the project's 4px spacing scale and existing radii:
- inputs/small controls: 6px;
- standard cards: 10px;
- large overlays only: 16px.
Do not introduce generic SaaS styling such as giant pill buttons, glassmorphism, gradients, glowing cards or excessive shadows.
User API-access page
Rework the API request section as a focused form rather than a horizontal toolbar.
Keep it within the brand guideline's approximately 760px maximum width for form-focused flows, rather than stretching the form across the page.
Desired structure:
API access
Supporting copy:
Request managed API capacity for an external application or integration.
Then place the fields vertically with clear spacing:
Consumer or application name
[ input ]
Add short supporting/helper text if existing product conventions support it, for example explaining that this should identify the application consuming the API.
Intended use
[ textarea ]
The textarea should be comfortably sized for several sentences rather than looking like a one-line field.
Then place the primary action below:
Request API access
This should use the proper primary-button treatment.
Requirements:
- Labels must remain visible above their fields.
- Do not use placeholders as substitutes for labels.
- Give fields a sensible width and height.
- Use consistent border, hover, focus, disabled and validation states.
- Preserve the existing functionality and API behaviour.
- If there are existing success/error messages, style them using the application's established system-state patterns.
- Prevent duplicate submissions while a request is processing if the existing logic supports a loading state.
Admin pending-request interface
Turn each pending API request into a clear review card/panel instead of presenting all information as loose text across the full viewport.
A request should have a hierarchy roughly like:
Pending API access requests
Then for each request:
Dev Testing
Requested by account 67 as secondary metadata
Used to test if feature works
A clearly separated Capacity section containing:
- Requests per minute
- Requests per UTC day
Use appropriately sized numeric inputs, preferably in a small responsive two-column grid on wider screens and stacked on narrow screens.
Then:
Review reason (optional)
textarea
Add useful helper text if appropriate, e.g. that this reason will be recorded with the review decision, but only if that is true according to the existing backend behaviour.
Finally provide a clearly separated action region:
Approve request — primary action
Reject request — destructive/secondary destructive action
Do not make both actions visually equal.
Approve should be the dominant primary action for the review region. Reject should use the application's destructive styling, but avoid using red text alone as the only indication that the operation is destructive.

# Statâ€™sTheGame Brand and Interface Guidelines

| Document information | Details               |

| Product              | Statâ€™sTheGame         |

> This document defines the approved visual identity and frontend presentation standard for Statâ€™sTheGame. Project-team approval of the design documents was confirmed during issue #191 on 19 August 2026. Future changes continue through the normal project issue and Pull Request process.

---

## 1. Purpose and project alignment

Statâ€™sTheGame is the user-facing identity for the projectâ€™s T20 cricket analytics platform.

The interface must support the projectâ€™s existing architectural boundaries rather than create a separate product model:

- the React frontend presents data and user journeys;
- the frontend obtains application data through the documented backend HTTP API;
- authoritative validation, authorisation, business rules and database access remain backend responsibilities;
- the API remains a first-class product rather than an implementation detail;
- the current event-data domain is T20 cricket, with Cricsheet as the approved historical data source;
- user-facing work must remain usable, responsive, accessible and consistent with the agreed design.

Relevant project documents:

- [System architecture](../architecture/system-architecture.md)
- [Repository structure](../architecture/repository-structure.md)
- [API overview](../api/overview.md)
- [Cricsheet T20 data](../data/cricsheet.md)
- [Testing strategy](../development/testing.md)
- [Project methodology](../project_methodology.md)
- [Git methodology](../git-methodology.md)
- [AI usage](../ai/usage.md)

This document covers visual and interaction design only. It does not override architecture, security, API, database, testing or project-methodology decisions.

---

## 2. Brand foundation

### 2.1 Brand idea

**The game, measured ball by ball.**

Statâ€™sTheGame should make event-derived cricket data feel immediate without making it feel unreliable or superficial.

### 2.2 Brand personality

The product should feel:

- **Fast** â€” appropriate for T20 cricket and responsive interaction.
- **Exact** â€” statistics are evidence, not decoration.
- **Confident** â€” strong visual hierarchy without exaggerated marketing language.
- **Technical** â€” appropriate for analysts and API consumers.
- **Accessible** â€” understandable to cricket followers who are not data specialists.
- **Distinctive** â€” recognisable without generic SaaS or generic sports styling.
- **Traceable** â€” the interface should reinforce that published figures come from underlying event data.

### 2.3 Brand keywords

**Explosive. Exact. Traceable.**

These words are a design test, not marketing copy. A screen that is energetic but makes values harder to interpret is not on-brand. A screen that is technically correct but visually lifeless is also incomplete.

### 2.4 Tagline

Primary tagline:

> **The game, measured ball by ball.**

Approved secondary lines:

- Every ball. Every stat.
- From delivery to decision.
- Cricket data with a source.

Avoid phrases such as:

- â€œunlock the future of cricketâ€;
- â€œrevolutionary insightsâ€;
- â€œsupercharge your gameâ€;
- â€œAI-powered cricket intelligenceâ€ unless AI is genuinely a user-facing feature and the claim is specifically justified.

---

## 3. Product name

### 3.1 Written name

Use:

**Statâ€™sTheGame**

In normal prose, use the curly apostrophe.

Technical contexts may use ASCII-safe forms:

```text
Plain-text fallback: Stat'sTheGame
Repository/package slug: stats-the-game
URL/route segment: statsthegame
Environment prefix: STATS_THE_GAME_
```

### 3.2 Capitalisation

The product name is constructed as:

```text
Statâ€™s + The + Game
```

Do not use:

```text
StatsTheGame
Stats the Game
Stat's the game
STATSTHEGAME
```

All-uppercase treatment is allowed only in designed display contexts such as compact navigation or promotional artwork.

---

## 4. Approved logo concept

The logo is based on the selected reference artwork and contains:

- a navy cricket-player silhouette;
- a large orange apostrophe-shaped cricket bat;
- a lime cricket ball;
- a lime curved motion trail;
- the Statâ€™sTheGame wordmark.

The **orange apostrophe-bat is the defining brand device**. It must remain visually dominant in all logo refinements.

The approved reference image is the authority for the player pose, bat shape, ball, motion trail and overall composition. Future logo work must trace or adapt that reference deliberately; it must not regenerate the player through an image model and treat the result as the same logo.

### 4.1 Theme treatment

#### Day Match / light backgrounds

Use:

- navy player and wordmark;
- orange apostrophe-bat;
- lime ball and motion trail;
- transparent background.

#### Night Match / dark backgrounds

Use:

- warm off-white player and wordmark;
- orange apostrophe-bat;
- lime ball and motion trail;
- transparent background.

The orange and lime brand accents remain consistent between themes.

### 4.2 Logo variants

The brand system requires:

1. **Full logo** â€” player mark plus wordmark.
2. **Player mark** â€” player, orange apostrophe-bat, ball and trail without the wordmark.
3. **Wordmark** â€” Statâ€™sTheGame wordmark without the player.
4. **Favicon** â€” simplified orange apostrophe-bat mark with sufficient transparent safe area.

### 4.3 Minimum sizes

| Asset       |     Minimum recommended digital size |
| ----------- | -----------------------------------: |
| Full logo   |                          180 px wide |
| Player mark |                           40 px wide |
| Wordmark    |                          140 px wide |
| Favicon     | 16 Ã— 16 px, using simplified artwork |

If detail becomes unreadable below these sizes, switch to the next simpler asset rather than shrinking the full logo further.

### 4.4 Clear space

For the full logo and player mark, keep clear space on all sides equal to approximately the width of the playerâ€™s head.

Do not allow:

- text;
- borders;
- navigation controls;
- chart labels;
- card edges;

to intrude into the clear-space area.

### 4.5 Favicon safe area

The favicon must never touch the edge of its square canvas.

Requirements:

- keep at least **14% transparent padding on every side**;
- keep the visible mark centred optically, not only mathematically;
- verify the favicon at 16 Ã— 16, 32 Ã— 32 and 48 Ã— 48;
- do not use the full player or wordmark at favicon size;
- do not allow shadows or outlines to extend beyond the safe area.

### 4.6 Incorrect logo use

Do not:

- replace the orange apostrophe-bat with a normal cricket bat;
- move the apostrophe away from the playerâ€™s hands;
- recolour the apostrophe-bat green, blue or white;
- replace the lime ball or trail with unrelated accent colours;
- stretch, squash, skew or arbitrarily rotate the logo;
- add shields, trophies, crossed bats or wickets;
- add permanent neon glows to the production artwork;
- place the logo over busy imagery without a solid supporting surface;
- retype the wordmark in a different font and present it as the logo;
- regenerate the logo and silently replace the approved artwork.

---

## 5. Logo file structure and naming

The documentation site and frontend are independently deployable, so each needs access to its own static brand assets.

The **canonical design assets** live under:

```text
docs/design/assets/logo/
```

The **frontend runtime copies** live under:

```text

```

Files with the same name in these two locations must represent the same approved artwork.

### 5.1 Canonical documentation assets

```text

```

The reference PNG is retained for traceability and future vector redrawing. It is not intended to be used as the normal application asset.

### 5.2 Frontend runtime assets

### 5.3 Asset URLs in the frontend

Examples:

### 5.4 Current artwork format

The current approved reference is raster artwork. If an SVG variant contains embedded raster data, it must not be described as a true vector redraw.

- proportions;

## 6. Theme strategy

Statâ€™sTheGame supports two equal themes:

1. **Day Match** â€” warm light theme.
2. **Night Match** â€” dark broadcast-inspired theme.

Both themes use the same:

- layout;
- spacing;
- typography hierarchy;
- controls;
- content;
- interaction behaviour.

### 6.1 Theme behaviour

On first visit:

```text
1. Use a stored user preference if one exists.
2. Otherwise use the operating-system preference.
3. Otherwise default to Day Match.
```

Requirements:

- provide a visible manual theme control;
- persist the userâ€™s manual selection;
- do not change theme automatically based on time of day;
- do not force Night Match for live matches;
- avoid pure white and pure black as the main page canvas.

Components must consume semantic design tokens instead of hard-coded theme-specific values.

## 7. Day Match palette

Day Match is warm, editorial and scorecard-inspired.

| Token                     | Name            | Hex       | Primary use                       |
| ------------------------- | --------------- | --------- | --------------------------------- |
| `--colour-canvas`         | Warm Canvas     | `#F5F2E9` | Page background                   |
| `--colour-surface`        | Scorecard Paper | `#FFFDF7` | Cards, forms, modals              |
| `--colour-surface-raised` | Pavilion Paper  | `#EEE9DC` | Secondary surfaces                |

| `--colour-text-secondary` | Commentary Ink  | `#52636A` | Supporting text                   |

- Use colour together with labels, icons or patterns for statuses.

## 8. Night Match palette

| ------------------------- | --------------- | --------- | --------------------------------- |
| `--colour-canvas`         | Night Match     | `#08121B` | Page background                   |

| ----------------------- | --------- | ----------- |
| Page background         | `#F5F2E9` | `#08121B`   |
| Card background         | `#FFFDF7` | `#101E2B`   |
| Raised surface          | `#EEE9DC` | `#162736`   |
| Primary text            | `#102026` | `#F6F8F2`   |
| Secondary text          | `#52636A` | `#B8C3CC`   |
| Muted text              | `#627078` | `#8EA0AF`   |
| Border                  | `#D9D3C4` | `#263847`   |
| Primary action          | `#5D7E00` | `#C7FF4A`   |
| Brand/high-impact event | `#E95A24` | `#FF6B35`   |
| Link/comparison         | `#007F9E` | `#20D5FF`   |

A typical screen should remain predominantly neutral:

- 70â€“80% canvas and surfaces;
- 15â€“20% text and structural contrast;
- 5â€“8% primary green/lime;
- 2â€“4% orange/cyan accents.

Do not colour every statistic.

---

## 10. Typography

### 10.1 Font families

| Role                                  | Font             |
| ------------------------------------- | ---------------- |
| Display headings and major statistics | Barlow Condensed |
| Interface and body text               | IBM Plex Sans    |
| API paths, IDs and technical values   | IBM Plex Mono    |

Approved weights:

```text
Barlow Condensed: 500, 600, 700
IBM Plex Sans: 400, 500, 600
IBM Plex Mono: 400, 500
```

Production font loading must be treated as a documented frontend dependency. Prefer package-managed or self-hosted fonts over an undeclared third-party runtime dependency.

### 10.2 Type scale

| Style           | Size / line-height | Weight | Typical use            |
| --------------- | ------------------ | -----: | ---------------------- |
| Display         | 64 / 64            |    700 | Live score             |
| Page heading    | 48 / 52            |    700 | Page title             |
| Section heading | 30 / 34            |    600 | Dashboard section      |
| Card heading    | 22 / 26            |    600 | Panel title            |
| KPI value       | 40 / 42            |    600 | Key statistic          |
| Body            | 16 / 24            |    400 | Main content           |
| Small body      | 14 / 20            |    400 | Supporting content     |
| Label           | 12 / 16            |    600 | Metadata               |
| Technical       | 13 / 20            |    400 | Endpoint, ID, checksum |

### 10.3 Typography rules

- Use tabular numerals for scores, rates and data tables.
- Use condensed typography for display values, not paragraphs.
- Use uppercase only for short labels and compact navigation.
- Keep normal body text at 16 px where practical.
- Do not make every number lime or green.
- Use IBM Plex Mono only where monospacing communicates meaning.
- The logo wordmark is artwork; do not recreate it using Barlow Condensed.

---

## 11. Layout and spacing

### 11.1 Spacing scale

Use a 4 px base unit:

```text
4, 8, 12, 16, 20, 24, 32, 40, 48, 64, 80
```

### 11.2 Recommended content widths

| Context                           | Maximum width |
| --------------------------------- | ------------: |
| Analytics application             |       1600 px |
| Documentation / long-form content |       1100 px |
| Form-focused flow                 |        760 px |
| Standard modal                    |    720â€“900 px |

### 11.3 Grid

Desktop analytical screens may use a 12-column grid.

Useful patterns include:

- 8 columns for primary match content and 4 for supporting events;
- 9 columns for charts and 3 for compact supporting tables;
- four equal KPI cards;
- full-width tables when comparison is the primary task.

### 11.4 Responsive behaviour

Use content-driven breakpoints. Starting values:

```text
Small:   below 640 px
Medium:  640â€“899 px
Large:   900â€“1199 px
Wide:    1200 px and above
```

Stack dashboard regions before shrinking typography below usable sizes.

---

## 12. Shape and surface language

### 12.1 Corners

| Element                   | Radius |
| ------------------------- | -----: |
| Inputs and small controls |   6 px |
| Standard cards            |  10 px |
| Large overlays            |  16 px |

Fully rounded pills are reserved for controls or statuses where the shape has a clear purpose.

### 12.2 Signature clipped corner

Featured match cards, logo tiles and selected hero surfaces may use one clipped bottom-right corner.

Do not apply clipped corners to every container.

### 12.3 Borders and elevation

- Use 1 px borders for structural separation.
- Use shadows to communicate elevation, not decoration.
- Day Match shadows are broad and low-opacity.
- Night Match shadows are restrained and dark.
- Avoid glowing card borders.
- Avoid glassmorphism as the standard card language.

### 12.4 Crease line

A 2â€“3 px line is a recurring visual device.

Appropriate uses:

- active navigation;
- selected KPI card;
- chart target or benchmark;
- score transition;
- section accent.

Do not use it between every row.

---

## 13. Core interface components

### 13.1 Buttons

#### Primary

Day Match:

```text
Background: Crease Green
Text: white
```

Night Match:

```text
Background: Powerplay Lime
Text: Night Match
```

Use one dominant primary action per local region.

#### Secondary

Use:

- surface background;
- visible border;
- primary text;
- primary-colour focus/hover treatment.

#### Destructive

Use error styling only for genuinely destructive actions.

Irreversible actions require confirmation.

### 13.2 Cards

Cards should:

- use solid surfaces;
- group related information;
- have a clear hierarchy;
- avoid unnecessary icons;
- use spacing before heavy shadows.

Do not create a card solely to place a border around one line of text.

### 13.3 Navigation

- Desktop may use a compact left rail or top navigation.
- Mobile navigation must remain understandable without relying only on icon familiarity.
- The active state uses a soft selected surface plus the crease-line accent.
- Navigation remains stable during page transitions.

### 13.4 Tables

- Left-align entity names.
- Right-align numeric values.
- Use tabular numerals.
- Use subtle row separators.
- Keep long table headers sticky where helpful.
- Support horizontal overflow deliberately on small screens.
- Do not turn every value into a badge.

### 13.5 Forms

- Keep labels visible above inputs.
- Placeholder text does not replace a label.
- Validation identifies the exact issue and location.
- Required/error state is not communicated by colour alone.
- Submission flows must show progress and actionable validation results.

### 13.6 Loading and system states

Every data-driven screen must have deliberate states for:

- loading;
- empty results;
- validation failure;
- general error;
- unauthorised access;
- unavailable/offline backend;
- partial data where the API explicitly supports it.

Do not use an indefinite full-page spinner where useful structure can be rendered immediately.

---

## 14. Cricket data visualisation

### 14.1 Chart palette

| Role                    | Day Match       | Night Match     |
| ----------------------- | --------------- | --------------- |
| Current/selected series | Crease Green    | Powerplay Lime  |
| Comparison series       | Analysis Cyan   | Review Cyan     |
| Historical/unselected   | Scorebook Grey  | Commentary Grey |
| Wicket/anomaly          | Boundary Orange | Boundary Orange |
| Invalid/error state     | Rejected Red    | Rejected Red    |

### 14.2 Chart rules

- Start with the analytical question, not the chart type.
- Avoid rainbow palettes.
- Use line style, marker shape or opacity in addition to colour.
- State units and ranges explicitly.
- Label decisive points directly where practical.
- Keep tooltips keyboard accessible where practical.
- Provide text equivalents for important conclusions.
- Do not delay access to data while a decorative animation completes.

### 14.3 Cricket-specific conventions

Approved visual patterns include:

- orange wickets or decisive events;
- green/lime for the selected innings or player;
- cyan for comparison data;
- a crease line for a target or benchmark;
- ordered delivery events entering in source order.

Do not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.

---

## 15. Motion system

### 15.1 Motion character

**Sharp acceleration, controlled stop.**

Motion should make the interface feel responsive rather than decorative.

### 15.2 Timing

| Interaction            |   Duration |
| ---------------------- | ---------: |
| Hover / press feedback |  90â€“140 ms |
| Tooltip / dropdown     | 140â€“180 ms |
| Card / row entry       | 180â€“240 ms |
| Page transition        | 220â€“320 ms |
| Chart reveal           | 300â€“500 ms |
| Modal opening          | 220â€“280 ms |

### 15.3 Easing

```css
--ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
--ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
```

### 15.4 Signature animations

#### Score update

1. Old value moves up by no more than 4 px and fades.
2. New value enters from below.
3. The crease line flashes once.
4. Total duration stays below 500 ms.

#### Delivery insertion

A new delivery enters with:

- 6â€“8 px vertical movement;
- short opacity transition;
- no layout-blocking delay.

#### Wicket

Use one orange pulse or narrow strike.

Do not shake the screen or use confetti.

#### Page transition

Fade and move the primary content by no more than 8 px.

Do not move persistent navigation.

#### Chart reveal

The selected line may draw left-to-right once on first appearance.

Filtering or refreshing data should update promptly rather than replay a long entrance sequence.

### 15.5 Motion restrictions

Do not:

- bounce cards continuously;
- use decorative parallax behind data;
- stagger a dashboard for long periods;
- animate every value on every render;
- block interaction while an animation finishes;
- change layout dimensions significantly on hover.

### 15.6 Reduced motion

Respect the userâ€™s reduced-motion preference:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}
```

---

## 16. Accessibility

Accessibility is a project requirement and must be designed in from the start.

The teamâ€™s UI target is **WCAG 2.2 AA** unless a stricter project requirement supersedes it.

### 16.1 Required practices

- Verify text/background colour contrast.
- Provide a visible keyboard focus state.
- Prefer semantic HTML before adding ARIA.
- Keep interactive controls keyboard operable.
- Do not communicate state by colour alone.
- Provide text alternatives for meaningful images.
- Respect reduced-motion preferences.
- Maintain usable touch targets.
- Support browser zoom without loss of function.
- Preserve table and chart meaning on small screens.
- Test light and dark themes independently.

### 16.2 Colour notes

The muted light-theme text token has been darkened to `#627078` so it remains suitable for normal-size text against the Warm Canvas.

Boundary Orange is a brand accent on light surfaces, not a normal small-text colour.

Status colours should normally be paired with readable neutral text rather than used as the only text colour.

### 16.3 Focus treatment

Use a clearly visible 2 px focus ring with a 2 px offset.

Preferred rings:

- Day Match: Crease Green or Analysis Cyan.
- Night Match: Powerplay Lime or Review Cyan.

---

## 17. Iconography and imagery

### 17.1 Icons

Use:

- simple outline icons;
- consistent stroke weight;
- consistent view-box sizing;
- labels or accessible names for critical actions.

Avoid mixing unrelated filled, outline and illustration styles.

### 17.2 Cricket imagery

Prefer:

- real data;
- scorecards;
- field diagrams;
- delivery trajectories;
- the approved player mark;
- licensed authentic photography where useful.

Avoid:

- generic trophy graphics;
- crossed bats;
- decorative shields;
- fake 3D cricket balls;
- arbitrary stadium imagery;
- AI-generated players presented as real athletes.

### 17.3 Photography

When photography is used:

- preserve authentic colours;
- give overlaid text a solid or sufficiently opaque surface;
- avoid heavy colour grading that competes with data;
- do not place the logo over a face or visually complex focal point.

---

## 18. Interface writing

The product voice is direct, informed and calm.

Good:

```text
Explore matches
View delivery data
Compare innings
Export dataset
Submission awaiting review
12 events failed validation
```

Avoid:

```text
Dive into the action
Unleash next-level insights
Oops! Something went wrong
Your data journey starts here
```

### 18.1 Error copy

Error messages should state:

1. what failed;
2. where it failed;
3. what the user can do;
4. whether data was accepted or published.

Example:

```text
Delivery 43 is missing a striker identifier.
No events from this submission were published.
Add the identifier and submit the corrected file.
```

### 18.2 Cricket terminology

Use recognised cricket terminology accurately.

If a term is likely to be unfamiliar to a general user, explain it with supporting copy or a tooltip rather than replacing it with vague language.

---

## 19. CSS design tokens

Use semantic variables as the frontend implementation baseline.

```css
:root {
  --font-display: 'Barlow Condensed', sans-serif;
  --font-body: 'IBM Plex Sans', sans-serif;
  --font-mono: 'IBM Plex Mono', monospace;

  --radius-sm: 6px;
  --radius-md: 10px;
  --radius-lg: 16px;

  --space-1: 4px;
  --space-2: 8px;
  --space-3: 12px;
  --space-4: 16px;
  --space-5: 20px;
  --space-6: 24px;
  --space-8: 32px;
  --space-10: 40px;
  --space-12: 48px;
  --space-16: 64px;

  --motion-fast: 120ms;
  --motion-standard: 200ms;
  --motion-page: 280ms;

  --ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
  --ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
}

:root,

  color-scheme: light;

  --colour-canvas: #f5f2e9;
  --colour-surface: #fffdf7;
  --colour-surface-raised: #eee9dc;
  --colour-surface-soft: #f8f5ed;
  --colour-border: #d9d3c4;

  --colour-text: #102026;
  --colour-text-secondary: #52636a;
  --colour-text-muted: #627078;

  --colour-primary: #5d7e00;
  --colour-primary-ink: #ffffff;
  --colour-primary-soft: #dff0a7;

  --colour-brand: #e95a24;
  --colour-data-accent: #007f9e;

  --colour-success: #3a8f57;
  --colour-warning: #c98500;
  --colour-error: #d64251;

}

### 19.1 Theme initialisation

Resolve the theme before the main application paints where practical to avoid a visible flash of the wrong theme.

Precedence:

```text
stored preference
â†’ operating-system preference
â†’ Day Match fallback
```

---

## 20. Implementation rules

- Components use semantic tokens rather than raw theme hex values.
- Theme selection belongs at application/provider level rather than inside individual cards.
- Shared component structure and behaviour remain identical across themes.
- New colours require a documented design reason.
- New animation patterns require review for consistency and reduced-motion behaviour.
- Use existing shared UI patterns before adding visually equivalent alternatives.
- User-facing changes must be checked for responsiveness and accessibility before being considered done.
- Brand assets must not contain secrets, runtime configuration or environment-specific URLs.
- The frontend must not use branding work as a reason to bypass the documented HTTP API boundary.

---

## 21. Anti-generic design checklist

Reconsider a design if it relies on several of the following:

- purple-to-blue SaaS gradients;
- floating glass cards;
- oversized pill buttons;
- decorative blobs;
- unexplained sparkles;
- generic trophies or shields;
- excessive icon use;
- lime text on every statistic;
- full-screen animation before useful content appears;
- fake AI sports imagery;
- identical card layouts for unrelated information;
- vague marketing copy;
- â€œOopsâ€ error messages;
- inconsistent corner radii;
- many unrelated accent colours.

Statâ€™sTheGame should be recognisable through:

- the approved player logo;
- the orange apostrophe-bat;
- the lime ball and motion trail;
- Day Match and Night Match;
- scoreboard-inspired typography;
- the crease-line device;
- strong numeric hierarchy;
- event-first visualisation;
- restrained fast motion.

---

## 22. Review checklist

- [ ] Product name is written correctly.
- [ ] Approved logo variant is used for the background.
- [ ] Orange apostrophe-bat remains recognisable.

### Interaction

- [ ] Motion is purposeful and fast.
- [ ] Reduced-motion behaviour works.
- [ ] Loading, empty and error states exist.
- [ ] Keyboard focus is visible.

### Accessibility

- [ ] Colour contrast has been checked.
- [ ] Colour is not the sole state indicator.
- [ ] Interactive controls have accessible names.
- [ ] Charts retain meaning without animation.
- [ ] Touch and keyboard interaction have been considered.

### Project consistency

- [ ] Frontend data still flows through documented backend endpoints.
- [ ] No authoritative business rule has been moved into presentation code.
- [ ] Relevant tests and documentation are updated.
- [ ] Work follows the project issue, branch, review and merge process.
- [ ] AI assistance is recorded where required.

---

## 23. Change control

Changes to any of the following should be treated as a deliberate design decision rather than a casual component tweak:

- product name;
- logo composition;
- player pose;
- apostrophe-bat shape;
- lime ball or motion trail;
- primary theme palettes;
- typography families;
- core motion language.

For a material change:

1. record the proposed change in a Gitea issue;
2. explain the motivation;
3. attach design evidence or comparison where appropriate;
4. obtain normal team review;
5. update this document and affected assets in the same Pull Request where practical.

Do not claim that a visual change has been approved until the relevant team review has actually occurred.

## 2. Brand foundation

**The game, measured ball by ball.**

**Explosive. Exact. Traceable.**

## 3. Product name

## 6. Theme strategy

Statâ€™sTheGame supports two equal themes:

1. **Day Match** â€” warm light theme.
2. **Night Match** â€” dark broadcast-inspired theme.

Both themes use the same:

- information architecture;
- layout;
- spacing;
- typography hierarchy;
- controls;
- content;
- interaction behaviour.

Theme switching changes colour and elevation only. It must not reveal, hide or move functionality.

### 6.1 Theme behaviour

On first visit:

1. Use a stored user preference if one exists.

Requirements:

- provide a visible manual theme control;
- persist the userâ€™s manual selection;
- do not change theme automatically based on time of day;
- do not force Night Match for live matches;
- avoid pure white and pure black as the main page canvas.

Components must consume semantic design tokens instead of hard-coded theme-specific values.

## 13. Core interface components

### 13.1 Buttons

#### Primary

Day Match:

```text

Text: white
```

Night Match:

```text

Text: Night Match
```

Use one dominant primary action per local region.

#### Secondary

Use:

- surface background;
- visible border;
- primary text;
- primary-colour focus/hover treatment.

#### Destructive

Use error styling only for genuinely destructive actions.

Irreversible actions require confirmation.

### 13.2 Cards

Cards should:

- use solid surfaces;
- group related information;
- have a clear hierarchy;
- avoid unnecessary icons;
- use spacing before heavy shadows.

Do not create a card solely to place a border around one line of text.

### 13.3 Navigation

- Desktop may use a compact left rail or top navigation.
- Mobile navigation must remain understandable without relying only on icon familiarity.
- The active state uses a soft selected surface plus the crease-line accent.
- Navigation remains stable during page transitions.

### 13.4 Tables

- Left-align entity names.
- Right-align numeric values.
- Use tabular numerals.
- Use subtle row separators.
- Keep long table headers sticky where helpful.
- Support horizontal overflow deliberately on small screens.
- Do not turn every value into a badge.

### 13.5 Forms

- Keep labels visible above inputs.
- Placeholder text does not replace a label.
- Validation identifies the exact issue and location.
- Required/error state is not communicated by colour alone.
- Submission flows must show progress and actionable validation results.

### 13.6 Loading and system states

Every data-driven screen must have deliberate states for:

- loading;
- empty results;
- validation failure;
- general error;
- unauthorised access;
- unavailable/offline backend;
- partial data where the API explicitly supports it.

Do not use an indefinite full-page spinner where useful structure can be rendered immediately.

Approved visual patterns include:

- orange wickets or decisive events;
- green/lime for the selected innings or player;
- cyan for comparison data;
- a crease line for a target or benchmark;
- ordered delivery events entering in source order.

Do not use an error colour simply because it matches a team kit.

## 15. Motion system

### 15.1 Motion character

**Sharp acceleration, controlled stop.**

Motion should make the interface feel responsive rather than decorative.

### 15.2 Timing

| Interaction            |   Duration |
| ---------------------- | ---------: |
| Hover / press feedback |  90â€“140 ms |
| Tooltip / dropdown     | 140â€“180 ms |
| Card / row entry       | 180â€“240 ms |
| Page transition        | 220â€“320 ms |
| Chart reveal           | 300â€“500 ms |
| Modal opening          | 220â€“280 ms |

### 15.3 Easing

```css
--ease-fast: cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
--ease-hit: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1);
```

### 15.4 Signature animations

#### Score update

1. Old value moves up by no more than 4 px and fades.
2. New value enters from below.
3. The crease line flashes once.
4. Total duration stays below 500 ms.

#### Delivery insertion

A new delivery enters with:

- 6â€“8 px vertical movement;
- short opacity transition;
- no layout-blocking delay.

#### Wicket

Use one orange pulse or narrow strike.

Do not shake the screen or use confetti.

#### Page transition

Fade and move the primary content by no more than 8 px.

Do not move persistent navigation.

#### Chart reveal

The selected line may draw left-to-right once on first appearance.

Filtering or refreshing data should update promptly rather than replay a long entrance sequence.

### 15.5 Motion restrictions

Do not:

- bounce cards continuously;
- use decorative parallax behind data;
- stagger a dashboard for long periods;
- animate every value on every render;
- block interaction while an animation finishes;
- change layout dimensions significantly on hover.

### 15.6 Reduced motion

Respect the userâ€™s reduced-motion preference:

```css
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *,
  *::before,
  *::after {
    animation-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 0.001ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
}
```

## 16. Accessibility

Accessibility is a project requirement and must be designed in from the start.

The teamâ€™s UI target is **WCAG 2.2 AA** unless a stricter project requirement supersedes it.

### 16.1 Required practices

- Verify text/background colour contrast.
- Provide a visible keyboard focus state.
- Prefer semantic HTML before adding ARIA.
- Keep interactive controls keyboard operable.
- Do not communicate state by colour alone.
- Provide text alternatives for meaningful images.
- Respect reduced-motion preferences.
- Maintain usable touch targets.
- Support browser zoom without loss of function.
- Preserve table and chart meaning on small screens.
- Test light and dark themes independently.

### 16.2 Colour notes

The muted light-theme text token has been darkened to `#627078` so it remains suitable for normal-size text against the Warm Canvas.

Boundary Orange is a brand accent on light surfaces, not a normal small-text colour.

Status colours should normally be paired with readable neutral text rather than used as the only text colour.

### 16.3 Focus treatment

Use a clearly visible 2 px focus ring with a 2 px offset.

Preferred rings:

- Day Match: Crease Green or Analysis Cyan.
- Night Match: Powerplay Lime or Review Cyan.

### 17.1 Icons

Use:

### 17.2 Cricket imagery

Prefer:

- field diagrams;
- delivery trajectories;
- the approved player mark;
- licensed authentic photography where useful.

Avoid:

- crossed bats;
- decorative shields;

- AI-generated players presented as real athletes.

When photography is used:

- do not place the logo over a face or visually complex focal point.

The product voice is direct, informed and calm.

Good:

```text
Explore matches

Avoid:

Error messages should state:

1. what failed;
2. where it failed;

Example:

```text

No events from this submission were published.
Add the identifier and submit the corrected file.
```

### 18.2 Cricket terminology

Use recognised cricket terminology accurately.

If a term is likely to be unfamiliar to a general user, explain it with supporting copy or a tooltip rather than replacing it with vague language.

## 20. Implementation rules

- Components use semantic tokens rather than raw theme hex values.
- Theme selection belongs at application/provider level rather than inside individual cards.
- Shared component structure and behaviour remain identical across themes.
- New colours require a documented design reason.
- New animation patterns require review for consistency and reduced-motion behaviour.
- Use existing shared UI patterns before adding visually equivalent alternatives.
- User-facing changes must be checked for responsiveness and accessibility before being considered done.
- Brand assets must not contain secrets, runtime configuration or environment-specific URLs.
- The frontend must not use branding work as a reason to bypass the documented HTTP API boundary.

Reconsider a design if it relies on several of the following:

- purple-to-blue SaaS gradients;
- floating glass cards;
- oversized pill buttons;
- decorative blobs;
- unexplained sparkles;
- generic trophies or shields;
- excessive icon use;
- lime text on every statistic;
- full-screen animation before useful content appears;
- fake AI sports imagery;
- identical card layouts for unrelated information;
- vague marketing copy;
- â€œOopsâ€ error messages;
- inconsistent corner radii;
- many unrelated accent colours.

Statâ€™sTheGame should be recognisable through:

- the approved player logo;
- the orange apostrophe-bat;
- the lime ball and motion trail;
- Day Match and Night Match;
- scoreboard-inspired typography;
- the crease-line device;
- strong numeric hierarchy;
- event-first visualisation;
- restrained fast motion.

---

## 22. Review checklist

### Brand

- [ ] Product name is written correctly.
- [ ] Approved logo variant is used for the background.
- [ ] Orange apostrophe-bat remains recognisable.
- [ ] Logo clear space is preserved.
- [ ] Favicon has at least 14% transparent safe area.

### Theme

- [ ] Screen works in Day Match.
- [ ] Screen works in Night Match.
- [ ] Components use semantic tokens.

### Layout

### Interaction

- [ ] Motion is purposeful and fast.
- [ ] Reduced-motion behaviour works.
- [ ] Loading, empty and error states exist.
- [ ] Keyboard focus is visible.

### Accessibility

- [ ] Colour contrast has been checked.
- [ ] Colour is not the sole state indicator.
- [ ] Interactive controls have accessible names.
- [ ] Charts retain meaning without animation.
- [ ] Touch and keyboard interaction have been considered.

### Project consistency

- [ ] Frontend data still flows through documented backend endpoints.
- [ ] No authoritative business rule has been moved into presentation code.
- [ ] Relevant tests and documentation are updated.
- [ ] Work follows the project issue, branch, review and merge process.
- [ ] AI assistance is recorded where required.

---

## 23. Change control

Changes to any of the following should be treated as a deliberate design decision rather than a casual component tweak:

- product name;
- logo composition;
- player pose;
- apostrophe-bat shape;
- lime ball or motion trail;
- primary theme palettes;
- typography families;
- core motion language.

For a material change:

1. record the proposed change in a Gitea issue;
2. explain the motivation;
3. attach design evidence or comparison where appropriate;
4. obtain normal team review;
5. update this document and affected assets in the same Pull Request where practical.

Do not claim that a visual change has been approved until the relevant team review has actually occurred.

# Statâ€™sTheGame Brand and Interface Guidelines

| Document information | Details               |
| -------------------- | --------------------- |
| Product              | Statâ€™sTheGame         |
| Domain               | T20 cricket analytics |
| Light theme          | Day Match             |
| Dark theme           | Night Match           |
| Document version     | 1.0                   |
| Status               | Approved              |
| Date                 | 7 August 2026         |
| Approval confirmed   | 19 August 2026        |

> This document defines the approved visual identity and frontend presentation standard for Statâ€™sTheGame. Project-team approval of the design documents was confirmed during issue #191 on 19 August 2026. Future changes continue through the normal project issue and Pull Request process.

---

## 1. Purpose and project alignment

Statâ€™sTheGame is the user-facing identity for the projectâ€™s T20 cricket analytics platform.

The interface must support the projectâ€™s existing architectural boundaries rather than create a separate product model:

- the React frontend presents data and user journeys;
- the frontend obtains application data through the documented backend HTTP API;
- authoritative validation, authorisation, business rules and database access remain backend responsibilities;
- the API remains a first-class product rather than an implementation detail;
- the current event-data domain is T20 cricket, with Cricsheet as the approved historical data source;
- user-facing work must remain usable, responsive, accessible and consistent with the agreed design.

Relevant project documents:

- [System architecture](../architecture/system-architecture.md)
- [Repository structure](../architecture/repository-structure.md)
- [API overview](../api/overview.md)
- [Cricsheet T20 data](../data/cricsheet.md)
- [Testing strategy](../development/testing.md)
- [Project methodology](../project_methodology.md)
- [Git methodology](../git-methodology.md)
- [AI usage](../ai/usage.md)

This document covers visual and interaction design only. It does not override architecture, security, API, database, testing or project-methodology decisions.

---

## 2. Brand foundation

### 2.1 Brand idea

**The game, measured ball by ball.**

Statâ€™sTheGame should make event-derived cricket data feel immediate without making it feel unreliable or superficial.

### 2.2 Brand personality

The product should feel:

- **Fast** â€” appropriate for T20 cricket and responsive interaction.
- **Exact** â€” statistics are evidence, not decoration.
- **Confident** â€” strong visual hierarchy without exaggerated marketing language.
- **Technical** â€” appropriate for analysts and API consumers.
- **Accessible** â€” understandable to cricket followers who are not data specialists.
- **Distinctive** â€” recognisable without generic SaaS or generic sports styling.
- **Traceable** â€” the interface should reinforce that published figures come from underlying event data.

### 2.3 Brand keywords

**Explosive. Exact. Traceable.**

These words are a design test, not marketing copy. A screen that is energetic but makes values harder to interpret is not on-brand. A screen that is technically correct but visually lifeless is also incomplete.

### 2.4 Tagline

Primary tagline:

> **The game, measured ball by ball.**

Approved secondary lines:

- Every ball. Every stat.
- From delivery to decision.
- Cricket data with a source.

Avoid phrases such as:

- â€œunlock the future of cricketâ€;
- â€œrevolutionary insightsâ€;
- â€œsupercharge your gameâ€;
- â€œAI-powered cricket intelligenceâ€ unless AI is genuinely a user-facing feature and the claim is specifically justified.

---

## 3. Product name

### 3.1 Written name

Use:

**Statâ€™sTheGame**

In normal prose, use the curly apostrophe.

Technical contexts may use ASCII-safe forms:

```text
Plain-text fallback: Stat'sTheGame
Repository/package slug: stats-the-game
URL/route segment: statsthegame
Environment prefix: STATS_THE_GAME_
```

### 3.2 Capitalisation

The product name is constructed as:

```text
Statâ€™s + The + Game
```

Do not use:

```text
StatsTheGame
Stats the Game
Stat's the game
STATSTHEGAME
```

All-uppercase treatment is allowed only in designed display contexts such as compact navigation or promotional artwork.

---

## 4. Approved logo concept

The logo is based on the selected reference artwork and contains:

- a navy cricket-player silhouette;
- a large orange apostrophe-shaped cricket bat;
- a lime cricket ball;
- a lime curved motion trail;
- the Statâ€™sTheGame wordmark.

The **orange apostrophe-bat is the defining brand device**. It must remain visually dominant in all logo refinements.

The approved reference image is the authority for the player pose, bat shape, ball, motion trail and overall composition. Future logo work must trace or adapt that reference deliberately; it must not regenerate the player through an image model and treat the result as the same logo.

### 4.1 Theme treatment

#### Day Match / light backgrounds

Use:

- navy player and wordmark;
- orange apostrophe-bat;
- lime ball and motion trail;
- transparent background.

#### Night Match / dark backgrounds

Use:

- warm off-white player and wordmark;
- orange apostrophe-bat;
- lime ball and motion trail;
- transparent background.

The orange and lime brand accents remain consistent between themes.

### 4.2 Logo variants

The brand system requires:

1. **Full logo** â€” player mark plus wordmark.
2. **Player mark** â€” player, orange apostrophe-bat, ball and trail without the wordmark.
3. **Wordmark** â€” Statâ€™sTheGame wordmark without the player.
4. **Favicon** â€” simplified orange apostrophe-bat mark with sufficient transparent safe area.

### 4.3 Minimum sizes

| Asset       |     Minimum recommended digital size |
| ----------- | -----------------------------------: |
| Full logo   |                          180 px wide |
| Player mark |                           40 px wide |
| Wordmark    |                          140 px wide |
| Favicon     | 16 Ã— 16 px, using simplified artwork |

If detail becomes unreadable below these sizes, switch to the next simpler asset rather than shrinking the full logo further.

### 4.4 Clear space

For the full logo and player mark, keep clear space on all sides equal to approximately the width of the playerâ€™s head.

Do not allow:

- text;
- borders;
- navigation controls;
- chart labels;
- card edges;

to intrude into the clear-space area.

### 4.5 Favicon safe area

The favicon must never touch the edge of its square canvas.

Requirements:

- keep at least **14% transparent padding on every side**;
- keep the visible mark centred optically, not only mathematically;
- verify the favicon at 16 Ã— 16, 32 Ã— 32 and 48 Ã— 48;
- do not use the full player or wordmark at favicon size;
- do not allow shadows or outlines to extend beyond the safe area.

### 4.6 Incorrect logo use

Do not:

- replace the orange apostrophe-bat with a normal cricket bat;
- move the apostrophe away from the playerâ€™s hands;
- recolour the apostrophe-bat green, blue or white;
- replace the lime ball or trail with unrelated accent colours;
- stretch, squash, skew or arbitrarily rotate the logo;
- add shields, trophies, crossed bats or wickets;
- add permanent neon glows to the production artwork;
- place the logo over busy imagery without a solid supporting surface;
- retype the wordmark in a different font and present it as the logo;
- regenerate the logo and silently replace the approved artwork.

---

## 5. Logo file structure and naming

The documentation site and frontend are independently deployable, so each needs access to its own static brand assets.

The **canonical design assets** live under:

```text
docs/design/assets/logo/
```

The **frontend runtime copies** live under:

```text
apps/frontend/public/brand/
```

Files with the same name in these two locations must represent the same approved artwork.

### 5.1 Canonical documentation assets

```text
docs/design/assets/logo/
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-logo-reference.png
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-logo-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-logo-dark.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-mark-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-mark-dark.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-wordmark-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-wordmark-dark.svg
â””â”€â”€ statsthegame-favicon.svg
```

The reference PNG is retained for traceability and future vector redrawing. It is not intended to be used as the normal application asset.

### 5.2 Frontend runtime assets

```text
apps/frontend/public/brand/
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-logo-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-logo-dark.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-mark-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-mark-dark.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-wordmark-light.svg
â”œâ”€â”€ statsthegame-wordmark-dark.svg

```

For broad browser compatibility, also provide:

```text
apps/frontend/public/favicon.ico
```

The `.ico` file must use the same padded apostrophe-bat artwork as the SVG favicon.

### 5.3 Asset URLs in the frontend

Examples:

```text

/brand/statsthegame-logo-dark.svg
/brand/statsthegame-mark-light.svg
/brand/statsthegame-mark-dark.svg
